---
title: "Figure essentials and colours"
description: >
  The conventions every bioToolkit plot shares: theme, fixed panel sizes,
  saving to PDF and PNG, legends, source data, gene names and colours.
---

```{r setup, include = FALSE}
source("_common.R")
```

Every plot of the package follows the same rules, so a figure made from one
function matches the others:

| | |
|---|---|
| **Theme** | `theme_bioToolkit()`: 11 / 9 / 12 pt text, 1 pt axes, bold legend titles, transparent background |
| **Size** | panels have a fixed size in inches (`panel.width`, `cell.width`, ...), whatever the legend or number of groups |
| **Saving** | `save_plot()` sizes the file to fit the plot; PDF (vector) or PNG at 1000 dpi |
| **Colours** | one `cols` argument: a palette name, or colours named by group / from low to high |
| **Gene names** | in italics, symbols used as given (check the case for the organism) |
| **Data** | `export_source_data()` writes the table behind any plot |

The examples use PBMCs from [Kang et al. 2018](https://doi.org/10.1038/nbt.4042)
(control or interferon-β, 8 donors; 8,000 cells), loaded by the guides' data helper;
any Seurat object works the same way.

```{r data}
pbmc <- docs_kang()
p <- DimPlot_bioToolkit(pbmc, group.by = "cell_type", label = TRUE)
p
```

## Theme

`theme_bioToolkit()` is used by all plots of the package and can be added to
any ggplot. Its `type` sets the layout. A small simulated table for the
examples:

```{r theme-data}
set.seed(1)
toy <- data.frame(
    x = rnorm(60),
    y = rnorm(60),
    group = rep(c("A", "B", "C"), 20)
)
```

### Layouts {.tabset .tabset-pills}

#### "axis"

Axis lines and ticks, no grid: scatter, volcano, MA, bar and PCA plots.

```{r theme-axis}
ggplot(toy, aes(x, y, colour = group)) +
    geom_point() +
    theme_bioToolkit("axis") +
    panel_size_theme(2)
```

#### "grid"

Light grid, rotated x labels, no axis titles: dot plots and heatmaps, whose
rows and columns are categories.

```{r theme-grid}
ggplot(toy, aes(group, cut(x, 4), colour = y)) +
    geom_point(size = 3) +
    theme_bioToolkit("grid") +
    panel_size_theme(1.2, 1.6)
```

#### "embedding"

No axes, room for the dimension arrows: UMAP and t-SNE.

```{r theme-embedding}
ggplot(toy, aes(x, y, colour = group)) +
    geom_point() +
    theme_bioToolkit("embedding") +
    panel_size_theme(2)
```

## Fixed panel sizes

A panel has the same size in every figure, whatever the length of the labels
or the size of the legend, so panels line up when figures are assembled. The
package's plots take the size in inches, in one of two ways:

| Argument | Plots | What it sets |
|---|---|---|
| `panel.width`, `panel.height` | continuous axes: embeddings, volcano, MA, PCA, scatter | the whole panel. Scatter-type panels are square by default, so `panel.width` alone resizes them |
| `cell.width`, `cell.height` | categories: dot plots, heatmaps, violins, multi-volcano | **one** column or row (one gene, one group). The panel is the number of columns × `cell.width` |

With cell sizes, a dot plot of 8 genes is twice as wide as one of 4, but a
dot, a gene name and the gap between genes are the same size in both, so
several dot plots in a figure match each other.

### Sizes {.tabset .tabset-pills}

#### `panel.width`

```{r size-panel}
DimPlot_bioToolkit(pbmc, group.by = "condition", panel.width = 2.5)
```

#### `cell.width`: 4 genes

```{r size-cell-4}
DotPlot_bioToolkit(
    pbmc,
    features = c("CD3E", "MS4A1", "CD14", "FCGR3A"),
    group.by = "cell_type"
)
```

#### `cell.width`: 8 genes

The same cells: the panel is twice as wide, every dot the same size.

```{r size-cell-8}
genes_8 <- c("CD3E", "CD8A", "NKG7", "MS4A1", "CD14", "FCGR3A", "FCER1A", "PPBP")
DotPlot_bioToolkit(pbmc, features = genes_8, group.by = "cell_type")
```

#### Larger cells

Larger cells make everything in them larger; dots scale with the cell size:

```{r size-cell-large}
DotPlot_bioToolkit(
    pbmc,
    features = c("CD3E", "MS4A1", "CD14", "FCGR3A"),
    group.by = "cell_type",
    cell.width = 0.3,
    cell.height = 0.25
)
```

#### Any ggplot

`panel_size_theme()` gives any ggplot the same behaviour:

```{r size-own}
ggplot(toy, aes(x, y)) +
    geom_point() +
    theme_bioToolkit() +
    panel_size_theme(panel.width = 3, panel.height = 1.5)
```

## Saving

`save_plot()` measures the plot and writes a file that fits it, with nothing
cropped and no white margin. The format comes from the extension.

```{r save, eval = FALSE}
save_plot(p, "cell_types.pdf")   # vector, for journals and editing
save_plot(p, "cell_types.png")   # 1000 dpi raster
save_plot(p, "cell_types.jpg")   # no transparency: saved on white
```

PDFs and PNGs are both written with cairo, which embeds the fonts in PDFs and
keeps a hyphen as a hyphen (base `pdf()` draws it as a wider minus sign). Both
use the same font, Arial by default; `family` picks another, e.g.
`save_plot(p, "cell_types.pdf", family = "Helvetica")`. A font set in the
theme (`base.family`) is kept.

Backgrounds are transparent by default (`bg = "transparent"` in every plot),
so figures can be placed on any slide or panel; `bg = "white"` gives an
opaque one. Patchworks keep the size of every panel:

```{r patchwork}
p_cond <- DimPlot_bioToolkit(
    pbmc,
    group.by = "condition",
    cols = c("grey60", "#B5338A")
)
p | p_cond
```

Dense layers (cells, genes of a volcano) are rasterized at 1000 dpi once a
plot has many points (`raster`, `raster.dpi`), so PDFs stay small while
axes and text stay vector.

## Legends as separate files

`extract_legend()` takes the legend out of a plot, for figures where one
legend serves several panels. By default the legend is exactly as drawn in
the plot; its arguments redraw it differently, with ggplot2's own legend
settings.

### Extracting {.tabset .tabset-pills}

#### As drawn

```{r legend-asis}
extract_legend(p)
```

#### `direction`

Keys in a row; several legends side by side:

```{r legend-horizontal}
extract_legend(p_cond, direction = "horizontal")
```

#### `title.position`

The titles to the left of the keys, here of a dot plot's two legends:

```{r legend-title}
p_dot <- DotPlot_bioToolkit(
    pbmc,
    features = c("CD3E", "MS4A1", "CD14"),
    group.by = "cell_type"
)
extract_legend(p_dot, title.position = "left")
```

#### Restyled

Any theme setting of the legend through `...`, e.g. smaller text, more space
between keys, two columns of keys (a ggplot2 guide):

```{r legend-restyled}
two_cols <- guide_legend(ncol = 2, override.aes = list(size = 3))
p_two_cols <- p + guides(colour = two_cols)
extract_legend(
    p_two_cols,
    legend.text = element_text(size = 8),
    legend.key.spacing.y = unit(2, "pt"),
    legend.key.spacing.x = unit(8, "pt")
)
```

#### Several legends

A plot with a colour bar and a size legend, e.g. a dot plot, gives both,
stacked or (`direction = "horizontal"`) side by side:

```{r legend-several}
extract_legend(p_dot, direction = "horizontal")
```

### Saving

Save the plot without its legend, and the legend on its own:

```{r legend-save, eval = FALSE}
leg <- extract_legend(p_cond)
save_plot(p_cond + theme(legend.position = "none"), "umap.pdf")
save_plot(leg, "umap_legend.pdf")
```

## Source data

Journals increasingly ask for the data behind each figure.
`export_source_data()` writes the table a plot is drawn from (to CSV, or one
sheet per plot of a patchwork to XLSX) and returns it:

```{r source-data}
src <- export_source_data(p_cond)
head(src[[1]], 3)
```

```{r source-data-save, eval = FALSE}
export_source_data(p | p_cond, "figure_2a.xlsx")
```

For expression plots of a Seurat object, the table records the assay and
layer the values came from.

## Gene names in italics

Plots of genes set their names in italics by default (`italic.genes = TRUE`)
and leave metadata (e.g. `nCount_RNA`) upright. For your own ggplots,
`italic_labels()` does the same for a discrete scale:

```{r italic}
df <- data.frame(
    feature = c("CD3E", "MS4A1", "nCount_RNA"),
    value = c(3, 2, 1)
)
gene_labels <- function(x) italic_labels(x, x != "nCount_RNA")
ggplot(df, aes(value, feature)) +
    geom_col(width = 0.6) +
    scale_y_discrete(labels = gene_labels) +
    theme_bioToolkit() +
    panel_size_theme(2, 1)
```

Symbols are drawn as given: human genes are upper case (`CD3E`), mouse and
rat genes title case (`Cd3e`). Check the case of your object's gene names
before passing features.

## Colours {#colours}

Every plot has one `cols` argument with a good default. It takes:

- for **groups** (cell types, conditions): a palette name, or colours named
  by group, or in the order of the group levels. The default is `"scanpy-20"`
  (up to 20 groups; `"scanpy-102"` beyond);
- for **continuous scales** (expression, scores, fold changes): a palette
  name, or colours from low to high, `c(low, high)` or `c(low, mid, high)`.

Diverging scales (z-scores, fold changes, NES) keep their centre colour at 0
and stretch each side to its own end: when values run from -1 to 3, -1 gets
the full low colour and 3 the full high colour, rather than -1 sitting in the
pale middle of a symmetric -3 to 3 scale. Colour depth is then comparable
within a side, not between sides; the colour bar shows where 0 is.

### Picking colours {.tabset .tabset-pills}

#### By name

```{r cols-name}
DimPlot_bioToolkit(pbmc, group.by = "cell_type", cols = "okabe-ito")
```

#### Named colours

Pick colours by index (see `show_palettes()` below), reorder them and name
them by group, so that each cell type keeps its colour in every figure:

```{r cols-named}
cell_cols <- bt_palette("scanpy-20")[c(1, 2, 3, 5, 4, 6, 7, 8)]
names(cell_cols) <- levels(pbmc$cell_type)
DimPlot_bioToolkit(pbmc, group.by = "cell_type", cols = cell_cols)
```

#### Continuous

```{r cols-continuous}
FeaturePlot_bioToolkit(
    pbmc,
    features = "ISG15",
    cols = c("grey90", "#B5338A")
)
```

### Browsing palettes

Every palette, with the index and hex code of each colour, its source and
the plots that use it by default, is on the
[Colour palettes](palettes.html) page. In R, `list_palettes()` lists the
palettes with their type and source; `show_palettes()` draws them with the
index of each colour (also your own colours, or a list of both), and
`bt_palette()` returns the colours. Add `_r` to any name to reverse it.

```{r list-palettes}
head(list_palettes("qualitative"))
```

```{r show-palettes, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 2.2}
show_palettes(c("scanpy-20", "okabe-ito", "npg"))
```

```{r show-own-colours, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 1.2}
show_palettes(list(mine = cell_cols, "okabe-ito"))
```

```{r bt-palette}
bt_palette("scanpy-20")[c(1, 3, 2)]
bt_palette("viridis", n = 5)
```

### Colour vision deficiency

About 8% of men have red-green colour blindness. `check_palette()` simulates
it and warns about pairs of colours that become hard to tell apart:

```{r check-palette, warning = TRUE}
check_palette(cell_cols)
```

### Other colour helpers

```{r colour-helpers}
# Weighted mix of colours
mix_colors(c("#2C5DA8", "#B5338A"))
mix_colors(c("#2C5DA8", "#B5338A"), weights = c(3, 1))
# Order by hue
sort_colors_by_hue(bt_palette("okabe-ito"))
# ggplot2's default hues
ggplot_colors(4)
```

`ggplot_colors()` reproduces ggplot2's default colours for `n` groups, e.g.
to keep the colours of plots made with Seurat's defaults. (It was called
`ggplotColours()` before 1.0.0; the old name still works, with a
deprecation warning.)
